prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on one clean idea: trap many atoms at the magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels between the two clock states, so that the Doppler and recoil shifts vanish while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. Katori made that proposal and gave the first demonstrations. Ye's group at JILA took it to the 1e-18 level and into the regime where spin-exchange interactions and many-body effects matter. The accuracy now makes gravitational time dilation visible over millimetres, constrains variation of constants and prepares a redefinition of the second. This is also a case where accurate atomic-structure theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order shifts) is part of the result. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others agree with each other and are compared across continents, which is the kind of reproducibility I trust. The two-person split is natural. In the opening ballots, seven of eight members ranked B010, four of them in their top three, and I would not rely on that as merit; the reasons above stand on their own.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, which every optical clock needs, and the 2012 prize covered ion control and the Al+ clock. A reasonable colleague can say that lattice clocks are an improvement in degree on that line, and that the redefinition of the second is not yet done, so the headline payoff is still ahead. There is also a credit problem on the clock side, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Hall, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups all contributed and none of them is in the credited names. Finally, I would admit that a clock is a measurement capability, not a surprise about nature, and my own taste leans toward discoveries that show something unexpected. I think the lattice clock still counts because it opens a new regime of controlled quantum many-body systems that can be read out with extreme precision.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B010 first as a new measurement capability that extended metrology by orders of magnitude, giving relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and a path to redefining the second. He finds the Katori and Ye pairing clean but not exhaustive, and he wonders whether clocks are distinct enough from the comb and ion prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the capability argument, and I would add that the earlier prizes did not contain the lattice idea. The comb gave a frequency counter for light and the 2012 prize gave single-ion control. Neither removes the trade-off between atom number and motional shifts, and magic-wavelength trapping does. I accept that the credit boundary is not exhaustive, but a prize does not need to be. I would write the citation around the lattice scheme, so that the ion-clock and comb contributors are not implicitly excluded or implicitly repeated.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B061) first, as an instrument-driven discovery that opened neutrino astronomy, and puts B010 second, citing thoroughly confirmed precision measurement. He worries that three-person attribution within a large collaboration is a real fairness problem.
responses.response: I take IceCube seriously. It is a real discovery in nature, and I defer to you and to Danielsson on how secure the source identification is. My reservation is the one you raise yourself. The diffuse flux is confirmed, but only a handful of sources are identified, and crediting Halzen, Karle and Spiering out of a collaboration of hundreds is harder than two names for the lattice clock, where the idea and the demonstration belong to two groups. For that reason I keep B010 ahead. I would not oppose B061 if the committee finds the attribution acceptable, and I think it should be the main competitor.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B041) first because it opened a new regime of light-matter interaction and became the standard platform for superconducting quantum processors. He declares closeness to that community and notes the proximity of the 2025 prize on circuits.
responses.response: I respect the physics. Strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single microwave photon is a clear experiment. But I worry about timing, as you do, since the 2025 prize was awarded to the same platform only a year ago, and the main credit is split between a theory proposal and two experimental lines with Girvin and Devoret outside the names. I would also separate the platform from the discovery: much of its present impact is quantum computing engineering, which I weigh less than a new fundamental capability. I therefore keep B041 outside my configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle graphene (B051) first, as a theory-to-experiment story in which Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands and Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated and superconducting states. He ranks B010 sixth.
responses.response: The prediction followed by the observation is attractive, and I accept that it started a field. Condensed matter is not my area, so I defer to you on whether the physics is as settled as it looks. What holds me back is that the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and the credit to Cao and to earlier twist theory is awkward. A discovery whose central explanation is unsettled is, to me, less ready than one where every systematic has been measured. I would keep B051 as a strong alternative for the committee, but I rank it behind B010 on maturity, not on importance.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B061) first as a discovery found in nature that opened a new window on the universe and answered the old cosmic-ray origin question, and he asks whether the credit belongs to people beyond the supplied three.
responses.response: I agree that new windows on the universe are among the best prizes, and that is why I find the choice difficult. My question to you is whether the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results are strong enough to say that the origin question has been answered, or only that a flux exists. If the committee is satisfied that the detection alone is the discovery, then the attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is the remaining point, and I would like the experts' report to say who was decisive.

uncertainties: Whether a majority of the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether the priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations is exactly as I remember it, and how much credit Ye's group has for the accuracy and many-body work compared with other national laboratories.
Whether the secure source-level evidence for IceCube is enough to change my ranking, since this is outside my own field.
Whether the redefinition of the second, still pending, should be treated as part of the case or kept separate from it.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and I work in attosecond physics, which is why B054 is relevant to me; that candidate is not on this shortlist. My own work is in atomic many-body theory, so I know the methods of precision atomic structure that underlie lattice clocks, but I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, RIKEN, JILA or the other candidates here that I can identify from my profile, so no specific conflict is apparent for B010. For B019, I know the ultracold-atom community only from a distance.
